The Avesta. The sacred scripture of Zoroastrianism, an ancient Persian religion founded by the prophet Zoroaster, also called Zarathustra. Written in the Avestan language, a now-extinct Iranian tongue, it comprises hymns, liturgies, and teachings that shaped one of history's first monotheistic faiths.

The Avesta survives in fragmentary form, with only about one-quarter of the original text remaining, mostly in liturgical portions called the Yasna. The language is closely related to early Sanskrit, suggesting a shared Indo-Iranian cultural heritage with Vedic peoples.

The text is divided into five main sections. The Yasna contains hymns and prayers; the Yashts are songs to divine beings; the Visperad includes hymns for ritual; the Vendidad provides law against demons; and there are miscellaneous fragments. Central to the Yasna are the 17 Gathas, songs believed by some scholars to be Zoroaster's own words, though authorship remains debated.

Core doctrines include dualism between Ahura Mazda, representing good, and Angra Mainyu, representing evil. The faith emphasizes free will and cosmic judgment. The term Zend refers to Aramaic-language commentaries added later; Zend-Avesta is the combined term for text and commentary.

The Avesta profoundly influenced Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, particularly in their concepts of heaven, hell, resurrection, and apocalypse. It influenced Jewish eschatology and concepts of afterlife during and after the Babylonian exile. Islamic theology absorbed Zoroastrian cosmological and ethical frameworks. The teachings of Zoroaster, the prophet whose words the Avesta preserves and transmits, echo through these major world religions.
